[![CI Status](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/actions/workflows/gradle.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/actions/workflows/gradle.yml)
![TAssist UI](docs/images/Ui.png)
TAssist is a desktop application for teaching assistants who manage
students across multiple modules and classes.
It is optimised for teaching assistants who prefer fast keyboard-based
commands while retaining the benefits of a graphical interface.
## Features
- Add, find, list and remove student records
- Store student numbers, names, email addresses and Telegram usernames
- Create, list and remove module classes
- Assign and unassign students from classes
- List students assigned to a class
- List classes assigned to a student by displayed index
- Save successful changes automatically

# TAssist Developer Guide
<!-- * Table of Contents -->
<page-nav-print />
## **Acknowledgements**
* This project is based on the [AddressBook-Level3](https://github.com/NUS-CS2103-AY2627-S1/tp).
* Libraries used: [JavaFX](https://openjfx.io/), [Jackson](https://github.com/fasterxml/jackson), [JUnit5](https://junit.org/), [PlantUML](https://plantuml.com/) (for diagrams).

* AI coding tools such as Claude Code and Codex were used to help write documentation, code and tests, and to assist in code review. All AI-assisted work was checked by the respective authors before being accepted.
* TAssist Icon is generated by ChatGPT.
## **Setting up, getting started**
Refer to the guide [_Setting up and getting started_](SettingUp.md).
## **Design**
### Architecture
<puml src="diagrams/ArchitectureDiagram.puml" width="280" />
The ***Architecture Diagram*** given above explains the high-level design of the App.
The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.
**Main components of the architecture**

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`UI`**](#ui-component): The UI of the App.
* [**`Logic`**](#logic-component): The command executor.
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**
The *Sequence Diagram* below shows how the components interact with each other for the scenario where the user issues the command `delete 1`.
<puml src="diagrams/ArchitectureSequenceDiagram.puml" width="574" />
Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),
* defines its *API* in an `interface` with the same name as the Component.
* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

For example, the `Logic` component defines its API in `Logic.java` and implements it in `LogicManager.java`. Other components interact with a component through its interface rather than its concrete class, preventing them from coupling to that component's implementation, as illustrated in the following partial class diagram.
<puml src="diagrams/ComponentManagers.puml" width="300" />
The sections below give more details of each component.
### UI component
The **API** of this component is specified in [`Ui.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/Ui.java)
<puml src="diagrams/UiClassDiagram.puml" width="900" alt="UI windows, panels, cards and their dependencies on Logic and Model"/>
The UI consists of a `MainWindow` containing `CommandBox`, `ResultDisplay`, `PersonListPanel`,
`AcademicClassListPanel`, and `StatusBarFooter`, and owning a `HelpWindow` created during construction.
Both list panels create cards for their displayed records: `PersonCard` for students and
`AcademicClassCard` for classes. These UI parts inherit from the abstract
`UiPart<T>` class, which captures common behavior among classes that represent visible GUI parts.

The `UI` component uses the JavaFX UI framework. The layouts of these UI parts are defined in matching `.fxml` files in `src/main/resources/view`. For example, [`MainWindow.fxml`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/blob/master/src/main/resources/view/MainWindow.fxml) specifies the layout of [`MainWindow`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/MainWindow.java).
The `UI` component,
* executes user commands using the `Logic` component.
* listens for changes to `Model` data so that the UI can be updated with the modified data.
* keeps a reference to the `Logic` component, because the `UI` relies on the `Logic` to execute commands.
* depends on classes in the `Model` component to display `Person` and `AcademicClass` objects and student attendance.
Student cards use `WrappingFlowPane` for contact details and tags. It calculates each child's
wrapped height using the proposed available width, and uses the same row calculation for layout.
This avoids sizing a newly created or recycled list cell using its previous width. Optional
Telegram details and empty tag groups remain unmanaged, so they do not reserve layout space.
`MainWindow` forwards primary mouse presses on each outer list panel, including its heading
and padding, to that panel's list through `requestFocus()`. The outer containers do not add
extra Tab stops. `ReadOnlyListView` handles arrow, page and Home/End scrolling independently
of row selection; normal Tab and Shift+Tab traversal remains available.
### Logic component
**API** : [`Logic.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/logic/Logic.java)
Here's a (partial) class diagram of the `Logic` component:
<puml src="diagrams/LogicClassDiagram.puml" width="550"/>
The sequence diagram below illustrates the interactions within the `Logic` component, taking `execute("delete 1")` API call as an example.
Rollback and command-history handling are omitted for clarity and explained later in
[What happens when saving fails](#what-happens-when-saving-fails) and
[Arrow key command history navigation](#arrow-key-command-history-navigation).
<puml src="diagrams/DeleteSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Interactions Inside the Logic Component for the `delete 1` Command" />
<box type="info" seamless>
**Note:** The lifeline for `DeleteCommandParser` should end at the destroy marker (X), but due to a limitation of PlantUML, the lifeline continues till the end of diagram.
</box>
How the `Logic` component works:

1. When `Logic` is called upon to execute a command, the command is passed to an `AddressBookParser` object, which in turn creates a parser that matches the command (e.g., `DeleteCommandParser`) and uses it to parse the command.
1. This results in a `Command` object (more precisely, an object of one of its subclasses e.g., `DeleteCommand`) which is executed by the `LogicManager`.
1. The command can communicate with the `Model` when it is executed (e.g. to delete a person).
Note that although this is shown as a single step in the diagram above for simplicity, the code can require several interactions between the command object and the `Model` to complete the operation.
1. The result of the command execution is encapsulated as a `CommandResult` object which is returned from `Logic` after saving succeeds.
Here are the other classes in `Logic` (omitted from the class diagram above) that are used for parsing a user command:
<puml src="diagrams/ParserClasses.puml" width="600"/>
How the parsing works:

* When called upon to parse a user command, the `AddressBookParser` class creates an `XYZCommandParser` (`XYZ` is a placeholder for the specific command name, e.g., `AddCommandParser`). The parser uses the other classes shown above to parse the user command and create an `XYZCommand` object (e.g., `AddCommand`). The `AddressBookParser` returns that object as a `Command` object.

* All `XYZCommandParser` classes, such as `AddCommandParser` and `DeleteCommandParser`, implement the `Parser` interface so they can be treated similarly where appropriate, for example during testing.
### Model component
**API** : [`Model.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/model/Model.java)
<puml src="diagrams/ModelClassDiagram.puml" width="800" />
The `Model` component,

* stores the address book data i.e., all `Person` objects (which are contained in a `UniquePersonList` object). A `Person` is uniquely identified by its `StudentNumber`: two persons are the same (`Person#isSamePerson()`) if they share a student number. In addition, each `Email` and (if provided) `Telegram` username must be unique across all persons.

* stores all `AcademicClass` objects in a `UniqueAcademicClassList`. Each class is identified by its `ModuleCode` and `ClassName` and references its assigned students as `Person` objects. Students can belong to multiple classes.

* stores `Attendance` records in `AddressBook`, with at most one record per student-class pair. Each record references one `Person` and one `AcademicClass` and stores their unique attended dates. Attendance history is separate from class membership: unassigning a student retains their history, while deleting the student or class removes the associated records. Editing either preserves the dates and updates the record's references.

* stores the `Person` objects selected by the current filter, such as search results, in a separate _filtered_ list. It exposes this list as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Person>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when the list changes.
* exposes the academic classes selected by the current filter as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<AcademicClass>` for the UI to observe.
* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (currently, just the GUI settings). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object.
* does not depend on any of the other three components (as the `Model` represents data entities of the domain, they should make sense on their own without depending on other components)
### Storage component
**API** : [`Storage.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/storage/Storage.java)
<puml src="diagrams/StorageClassDiagram.puml" width="550" />
The `Storage` component,
* can save both address book data and user preference data in JSON format, and read them back into corresponding objects.
* is implemented by `StorageManager`, which delegates the actual JSON file access to `JsonAddressBookStorage` and `JsonUserPrefsStorage` (one class per data file).
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component (because the `Storage` component's job is to save/retrieve objects that belong to the `Model`)
### Common classes
Classes used by multiple components are in the `seedu.address.commons` package.
## **Implementation**
This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.
### Listing students by class
The `listbyclass` command displays students assigned to the class at a one-based index in the currently displayed
class list, not necessarily the full stored class list.
It optionally accepts a positive attendance threshold and displays only class members with fewer than that many
recorded attendance dates for the selected class. Students with no attendance recorded for the class have a count of
zero; dates recorded for other classes do not contribute. Without a threshold, all members are displayed.
It changes the student view, not the stored student records, class memberships, or the current class view.
The following sequence diagram traces `listbyclass 1 t/5`, assuming CS2103 (F10-2) is the first displayed class,
the selected threshold is 5, and saving succeeds.
It starts at `LogicManager`, omitting the UI caller. The input strings are defined in the diagram note.
`m:ModelManager` is accessed through the `Model` interface.

<puml src="diagrams/ListByClassSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Successful listbyclass execution with an attendance threshold, from parsing through class filtering, attendance display and result creation" />
1. `LogicManager` passes `commandText` to `AddressBookParser`, which creates a `ListByClassCommandParser`
and calls `parse(args)`. The parser tokenizes the optional `t/` prefix and uses
`ParserUtil#parseIndex(argMultimap.getPreamble())` for the displayed class index. It rejects duplicate `t/`
prefixes and, if a threshold is present, uses `ParserUtil#parsePositiveInteger(...)` to validate it.
It creates a `ListByClassCommand` with the index and optional threshold.
2. `LogicManager` captures a rollback snapshot before calling `execute(model)` on the command.
The command obtains the currently displayed classes through
`Model#getFilteredAcademicClassList()`, checks the index against the list size, and selects the class using
`lastShownList.get(index.getZeroBased())`.
3. The command calls `Model#filterPersonsByClassAndDisplayAttendance(academicClass, threshold)`. `ModelManager`
combines the class-membership predicate with the optional threshold predicate, using attendance counts for the
selected class. It also selects the class for attendance display and sorts matching students alphabetically with
`PersonNameComparator`. Name comparison ignores case, with original spelling as a tie-breaker. The student storage
order and current class view are unchanged.
4. The command obtains the displayed student list and uses its size, the class identity, and the optional threshold
to construct the success message. With `t/5`, it reports `Listed N students taking CS2103 (F10-2) with fewer
than 5 recorded attendance dates.` It returns a `CommandResult` to `LogicManager`.
5. `LogicManager` updates command history and saves the address book before returning the result,
even though this command only changes the view.
The view filter itself is not persisted.
The diagram summarises index and threshold parsing, class selection, and the combined model call. It omits
model-internal filtering and refresh calls, logging, list-size and class-field
access, message formatting, rollback snapshots, history updates and storage calls to keep the successful path readable.
**Other outcomes:** Missing, non-integer, zero, negative, or overflowing indices cause a `ParseException` before
command creation. A malformed, zero, negative, or overflowing threshold is also rejected before command execution.
A positive index beyond the displayed class list (including when that list is empty) causes a `CommandException`
before the student filter or attendance display changes. A valid class with no matching students succeeds: the student
view becomes empty and the result reports zero students. If saving fails after filtering, `LogicManager` reports a
`CommandException` and restores the previous display state and command history.
### Recording and removing attendance
The `addattendance STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX d/YYYY-MM-DD` and
`deleteattendance STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX d/YYYY-MM-DD` commands update one attended date for a student-class pair.
Both indices refer to the current displayed lists, which may be filtered independently. They are resolved when
the command executes, rather than against the full stored lists during parsing.
`Attendance` represents the association between a `Person` and an `AcademicClass`. It stores unique attended dates
in a `TreeSet<LocalDate>` and derives the attendance count from the set size. `AddressBook` owns the records and
resolves their endpoints to stored students and classes. Membership eligibility is command policy: additions
require the student to be assigned to the class, but removals can correct retained history after unassignment.
#### Recording a date
The following success path uses `addattendance 1 2 d/2024-02-29`. The selected student is assigned to the selected
class, the date is not in the future, and it has not already been recorded for that pair.

<puml src="diagrams/AddAttendanceSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Successful addattendance execution from parsing and displayed index selection through membership validation, recording a date and refreshing the student view" />
[Open the recording diagram at full size](diagrams/AddAttendanceSequenceDiagram.png).
1. `LogicManager` calls `AddressBookParser#parseCommand(commandText)`, which delegates to
`AddAttendanceCommandParser#parse(args)`. `AttendanceParserUtil#parseArguments` rejects unknown or duplicate
prefixes and requires `d/`. `ParserUtil#parseIndices` parses exactly two positive indices;
`ParserUtil#parseAttendanceDate` validates the calendar date. The parser creates an `AddAttendanceCommand`.
2. The command obtains `Model#getFilteredPersonList()`, validates the student index and selects the student.
It then obtains `Model#getFilteredAcademicClassList()`, validates the class index and selects the class.
It checks membership before attempting to record attendance.
3. The command calls `Model#addAttendance(person, academicClass, date)`. `ModelManager` delegates to
`AddressBook`, which reuses the pair's record or creates one if none exists. `Attendance#addDate` rejects
future dates using the computer's local calendar date and returns whether the date was newly added.
4. On success, `ModelManager#refreshFilteredPersonList()` re-evaluates the existing predicate and recomputes
attendance counts when a class threshold is active. Filters and ordering are retained, but students who
reach the threshold disappear and displayed indices may shift. The UI observes the list and refreshes its cards.
5. The command returns a success `CommandResult`. `LogicManager` updates command history and saves the address
book through `Storage` before returning the result.
#### Removing a date
The following success path uses `deleteattendance 1 2 d/2024-02-29`. The date is already recorded for the selected
student-class pair. The student and class still exist, but current membership is not required.

<puml src="diagrams/DeleteAttendanceSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Successful deleteattendance execution from parsing and displayed index selection through removal of a recorded date and student view refresh" />
[Open the removal diagram at full size](diagrams/DeleteAttendanceSequenceDiagram.png).
1. `DeleteAttendanceCommandParser` uses the same argument, index and date parsing helpers, then creates a
`DeleteAttendanceCommand`. The command validates and resolves the displayed student and class indices in that order.
2. The command calls `Model#removeAttendance(person, academicClass, date)` without a membership check.
`ModelManager` delegates to `AddressBook`, which resolves stored endpoints and locates their attendance record.
`Attendance#removeDate` removes only the specified date and returns whether it existed.
3. A successful removal triggers the same student-view refresh as an addition. Other histories and memberships
are unchanged. Removing the last date leaves a zero count; it does not delete the student or class.
4. The command returns a success `CommandResult`, and `LogicManager` updates command history and saves the address book.
Both diagrams follow the existing Logic/Model colours and start at `LogicManager`, omitting the UI caller.
The constructor arguments denote the parsed student index, class index and date. Parser helpers, list indexing,
membership inspection, private command helpers, model internals, logging, rollback snapshots, history and storage calls are summarised
in notes rather than shown as additional lifelines. `ModelManager` is accessed through the `Model` interface.
#### Validation, persistence and lifecycle
* Invalid argument structure, non-positive or overflowing indices, and malformed or impossible dates cause a
`ParseException` before command creation. Date syntax uses years `0001` to `9999`; future-date eligibility is
checked by the model during execution, not by the parser.
* An index beyond its displayed list, including an empty list, causes a `CommandException` before mutation.
Adding attendance for an unassigned student also fails before mutation.
* A duplicate addition or an absent date on removal returns `false` from the model; the command converts it
into a `CommandException`. Model `IllegalArgumentException`s, including future-date errors, are also converted
into command failures. Rejected operations do not change attendance.
* Previously recorded dates remain removable after a clock rollback or timezone change, even if they now appear
to be in the future. An unrecorded future date is rejected. Storage restores history through
`Attendance#fromRecordedDates` without applying today's date as a new-entry restriction.
* `JsonAdaptedAttendance` and `JsonSerializableAddressBook` persist the association and dates. Student and class
edits preserve history by rebinding the association; unassignment retains it, while deletion of either endpoint
removes the associated records. Reassignment can reuse retained history.
* If saving fails after a successful command mutation, `LogicManager` reports a `CommandException` and restores
the previous attendance data, display state and command history. A partial write may still leave the saved file incomplete.
The parser and command tests cover invalid input and duplicate/missing dates. `AttendanceIndexTest` covers
independently filtered panels and displayed bounds, while `AttendanceLifecycleTest` covers edits, deletion,
unassignment/reassignment, clock-related history handling and save/reload.
### Listing all classes
The `listclass` command restores the complete academic-class list by applying
`PREDICATE_SHOW_ALL_ACADEMIC_CLASSES`. It takes no arguments and leaves the
student list unchanged.
The following sequence diagram shows the successful execution of `listclass`.
Parsing helpers, model-internal predicate updates, result construction, and
storage calls are shown at a high level or omitted for clarity.
<puml src="diagrams/ListClassSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Successful listclass execution through the Logic and Model components" />
### Adding an academic class
#### Implementation

The `addclass` command creates an empty `AcademicClass`, identified by its `ModuleCode` and `ClassName`. `AddressBook` stores academic classes in a `UniqueAcademicClassList`, which rejects duplicate module code and class name pairs.
Given below is an example usage scenario for `addclass m/CS2103 c/F10-2`, assuming the class does not already exist.
Step 1. The user enters `addclass m/CS2103 c/F10-2`. `LogicManager` passes this command text to `AddressBookParser`, which creates an `AddClassCommandParser`.
Step 2. The command parser checks the arguments and uses `ParserUtil` to construct the `ModuleCode` and `ClassName`. It creates an empty `AcademicClass` and wraps it in an `AddClassCommand`.

Step 3. `LogicManager` executes the command. The command calls `Model#hasAcademicClass()` to check for an existing class with the same identity, then calls `Model#addAcademicClass()` when the class is absent.

The following sequence diagram shows how this operation goes through the `Logic` component. `commandText` is `"addclass m/CS2103 c/F10-2"`, `arguments` is `" m/CS2103 c/F10-2"`, and `a` is the class created by the command parser. The parsing helper calls, creation of `a`, and construction of the `CommandResult` are omitted for clarity.
<puml src="diagrams/AddClassSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Adding an academic class through the Logic component" />

Step 4. `ModelManager` delegates the addition to `AddressBook`. `AddressBook` copies the current academic class list, appends the new class, and passes the updated list to `UniqueAcademicClassList#setAcademicClasses()`. It then registers the class as a student observer so its membership can track student updates.
Similarly, the model sequence diagram below expands the `addAcademicClass(a)` call from the logic diagram:
<puml src="diagrams/AddClassSequenceDiagram-Model.puml" alt="Adding an academic class through the Model component" />

Step 5. The command returns a successful `CommandResult` with the message `New class added: CS2103-F10-2`. `LogicManager` saves the updated address book through `Storage` before returning the result to the UI. Storage calls are omitted from the logic diagram.
<box type="info" seamless>

**Note:** The logic diagram shows both successful addition and duplicate-class rejection. The model diagram expands only the successful addition. Invalid arguments cause a `ParseException` before the command is created. If `Model#hasAcademicClass()` returns `true`, the command throws a `CommandException` without adding the class. Neither failure reaches the save operation.
</box>
### Deleting an academic class

The `deleteclass` command identifies an existing class by its one-based index in the currently displayed class list. `AddressBookParser` delegates argument validation to `DeleteClassCommandParser`, which uses `ParserUtil.parseIndex()` and creates a `DeleteClassCommand` containing an `Index`. At execution time, the command retrieves `Model#getFilteredAcademicClassList()`, checks the index against its size, and calls `Model#deleteAcademicClass()` with the selected stored class. This is the same observable list used by the class panel, so selection respects the current class filter and display order. Invalid indices are rejected without changing the model.

The following diagram shows a successful run of `deleteclass 1`, assuming at least one class is displayed. The first displayed class is removed and the returned feedback identifies the deleted class. The existing model deletion path removes its assignments and attendance records while retaining student records. Remaining displayed classes are renumbered automatically. Parsing helpers and result construction are omitted for clarity; `LogicManager` saves the updated address book before returning the result to the UI. No storage schema or model interface change is required for index-based selection.
<puml src="diagrams/DeleteClassSequenceDiagram-Logic.puml" alt="Deleting an academic class through the Logic component" />

Invalid arguments cause a `ParseException` before command creation. If the class is absent, the command throws a `CommandException` without deleting anything. These error paths are omitted from the diagram.
### Assigning and unassigning students
`AssignCommand` and `UnassignCommand` change a student's membership in one academic class without
adding or deleting student records or classes. `AssignCommand` and `UnassignCommand` accept student and class indices in their respective
displayed lists, with the student index first. Hidden records cannot be selected.
#### Assigning a student
For example, `assign 1 2` assigns an existing student to an existing class.
The following sequence diagram starts at `LogicManager#execute(commandText)` and shows successful
parsing, command creation and execution. Here, `commandText` is the example above and `args` is
the argument string after the command word. Constructor arguments are abbreviated as `...`;
the parser passes the two validated displayed indices to the command.
`m:ModelManager` is accessed through the `Model` interface. The `Assign membership (model)`
reference frame is expanded in the next diagram.
<puml src="diagrams/AssignSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Successful execution of AssignCommand, resolving the displayed student and class through Model before assigning membership" />
1. `LogicManager` asks `AddressBookParser` to parse the input. It creates an `AssignCommandParser`,
which validates the arguments and constructs an `AssignCommand`.
2. `LogicManager` executes the returned command, which resolves the `Person` and `AcademicClass`
through `Model#findDisplayedPerson` and `Model#findDisplayedAcademicClass`. These lookups
encapsulate displayed-list access and bounds checks; the command reports invalid indices for empty results.
3. The command calls `Model#assignStudentToClass(person, academicClass)`.
4. On successful membership addition, the command returns a `CommandResult` to `LogicManager`,
which saves the address book before returning the result to its caller.
The following model-level sequence expands the membership update. The return value is `true`
for this scenario because the student was not already a member.
<puml src="diagrams/AssignSequenceDiagram-Model.puml" alt="ModelManager delegates assignment to AddressBook and AcademicClass adds the student to its membership set" />
`ModelManager` delegates to `AddressBook`, which checks the stored-object preconditions using
assertions before calling `AcademicClass#assignStudent(person)`. The class uses a set to prevent
duplicate membership. If the student is already assigned, the model returns `false` and
`AssignCommand` throws a `CommandException` instead of returning success feedback.
#### Unassigning a student
For example, `unassign 2 1` removes the second displayed student from the first displayed class.
The following sequence diagram starts at `LogicManager#execute(commandText)`, where `commandText`
is the example above. It assumes that both records exist and the student belongs to the class.
The parser validates exactly two positive indices using `ParserUtil#parseIndices`.
The command resolves the student through `Model#getFilteredPersonList()` and the class through
`Model#getFilteredAcademicClassList()`, checking each index against its displayed list size.
Membership changes go through the `Model` interface.
<puml src="diagrams/UnassignSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Successful execution of UnassignCommand, resolving displayed student and class indices before requesting removal through Model" />
1. `LogicManager` asks `AddressBookParser` to parse the input. It creates an `UnassignCommandParser`,
which validates the arguments and constructs an `UnassignCommand`.
2. `LogicManager` executes the returned command, which validates both displayed indices and
resolves the selected student and class.
3. The command calls `Model#unassignStudentFromClass(person, academicClass)` and checks whether
the model reports a successful removal.
4. A successful removal produces a `CommandResult`, which `LogicManager` returns after saving
the address book.
The `Unassign membership (model)` reference frame is expanded below. Only the selected class's
student set changes; the student record and memberships in other classes remain intact.
<puml src="diagrams/UnassignSequenceDiagram-Model.puml" alt="ModelManager delegates unassignment to AddressBook and AcademicClass removes the student from its membership set" />
If the student is not assigned to the class, `AcademicClass#unassignStudent(person)` returns `false`
without changing membership. This result propagates through the model to the command, which throws
a `CommandException`. Successful removal refreshes membership-dependent
student and class filters without resetting the active filters or ordering. Indices may shift as
records disappear from filtered views. Attendance history is retained for correction or reassignment.
#### Validation and failure paths
The activity diagram below complements the successful-execution sequence diagrams. Assignment
and unassignment both resolve displayed indices and validate the selected records before updating
membership and saving.

<puml src="diagrams/AssignUnassignActivityDiagram.puml" alt="Assign and Unassign workflow showing invalid input, missing student or class, unchanged membership, save failure and successful completion" />
The guards distinguish successful and rejected paths. An unchanged membership means that the
student is already assigned for `assign`, or is not assigned for `unassign`. In either case, the
command reports an error before `LogicManager` reaches the saving step. A failure to save after
a successful membership change is different: the in-memory change has already occurred.
#### Revealing affected records
Before calling `Logic#execute`, `MainWindow` captures the displayed student for `assign` and
`unassign`, and the stored class position. After successful execution, it locates each target
in its updated displayed list and calls `PersonListPanel#scrollToStudent` and
`AcademicClassListPanel#scrollToClass`. Both methods ignore out-of-range indices, including
`-1` for a target that has disappeared from a membership-dependent filter. This preserves
filters and ordering without revealing a replacement row. Typing and rejected commands do not
scroll either panel; the reveal methods do not change keyboard focus or selection.
#### Validation, errors and persistence
The sequence diagrams focus on successful execution and omit individual parser validation calls,
assertion lookups, formatting helpers and exception construction to keep the interactions readable.
* Both parsers reject anything other than exactly two positive integer indices, including prefixed input.
Both report `ParseException` before constructing the command.
* Both commands report an invalid displayed student or class index with `CommandException`,
including when the relevant view is empty.
Both resolve the student before the class, before attempting a membership update.
* A duplicate assignment or an absent membership is rejected without changing memberships.
* On successful command execution, `LogicManager` saves the address book before returning the
result to its caller. Saving occurs outside the scope of these diagrams. If saving fails,
`LogicManager` reports a `CommandException`; the in-memory membership change is rolled back.
A partial write may still leave the saved file incomplete.
### Arrow key command history navigation
Arrow key navigation lets users recall previously executed commands without executing them again. `CommandBox` delegates
history storage and navigation to its `CommandHistory`, which holds two separate lists and tracks the draft and the
current browsing position.
Up moves towards older entries and Down moves towards the draft (newer entries).
Navigation stops at either boundary, and empty history leaves the input unchanged.
Modified arrow keys (such as Shift+Up or Ctrl+Down) do not trigger history navigation.
`AddressBook` stores the latest 20 successful command strings, serialized as `commandHistory` in the existing JSON file.
`LogicManager` appends each successful command before saving and restores the previous history if saving fails.
History survives `clear` and application restarts. Older JSON files without this field load with empty history.
`MainWindow` seeds `CommandBox` through `Logic.getCommandHistory()` on startup; drafts, browsing positions and temporary
edits remain in memory only.
<puml src="diagrams/CommandHistoryObjects.puml" alt="CommandBox linked to CommandHistory, its draft and position, and its original and working command lists" />
| Field | Purpose |
| `commands` | Stores up to 20 successful commands in execution order, oldest first. Editing past commands does not change these entries. |
| `workingCommands` | Holds a working copy of the history. Temporary edits remain available until the next non-blank command submission, whether it succeeds or fails. |

| `draft` | Preserves the input from before the user started browsing history. Moving Down past the newest entry restores it. It is separate from the lists because it has not been successfully executed. |
| `position` | Identifies the selected entry in `workingCommands`, using a zero-based index. A value equal to the list size represents the draft. |
In the diagram, `position = 2` selects `list`. With four history entries, position 4 represents the draft. Moving Down past `find Alice` restores `addclass m/CS2103 n/f`.
#### Preserving temporary edits with two command lists
`commands` preserves the successfully executed commands. `workingCommands` is a separate list that preserves temporary
edits while browsing history. These partial object diagrams show only the two lists, with entries numbered from zero.
**Step 1: Recall.** After executing `help`, `find Carol`, `list`, and `find Alice`, the user presses Up to recall `find Alice`.
Both lists contain the same commands.
<puml src="diagrams/CommandHistoryBeforeEdit.puml" alt="CommandHistory with identical original and working lists before editing a recalled command" />
**Step 2: Edit and navigate away.** The user changes the input to `find Bob` without executing it, then presses Up to recall
`list`. Before moving, `saveCurrentInput()` saves `find Bob` in `workingCommands`. The original list still contains `find Alice`.
<puml src="diagrams/CommandHistoryAfterEdit.puml" alt="CommandHistory with a temporary edit in the working list while the original list remains unchanged" />
Pressing Down now recalls **`find Bob`**, so the user can continue editing it. Using a single list would either overwrite
the original history entry or lose the temporary edit. After a successful or failed submission, `resetNavigation()`
rebuilds `workingCommands` from `commands`, discarding temporary browsing edits.
A successful submission first adds the command to `commands` and clears the draft. A failed submission preserves the
failed input as the draft without adding it to history. Both cases reset `position` to the draft position.
### Preventing multiple TAssist instances
If two copies of TAssist run from the same folder, each keeps its own data in memory, so saving in one can overwrite changes saved by the other.
Therefore, TAssist only allows one instance per folder.
Before launching JavaFX, `Main#launchWithLock(...)` calls `ApplicationLock#tryAcquire(...)` to obtain

an operating-system lock on `tassist.lock` in the application folder. This uses [`FileChannel#tryLock()`](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/nio/channels/FileChannel.html#tryLock())
to reject another TAssist launch from the same folder. If the lock is already held or cannot be accessed,
`Main` prints an error and does not launch the application.
The lock is held while TAssist runs and released when the application exits.
Other applications can still modify `data/addressbook.json`. This is a [known issue documented in the User Guide](UserGuide.md#known-issues)
and should be addressed in future iterations.
### What happens when saving fails
Before executing a parsed command, `LogicManager#execute(...)` calls `Model#createRollback()` to capture
the current address book data and display state. After execution, it updates command history and saves the data.
The command result is returned only after saving succeeds.
The following activity diagram summarises this flow, assuming command parsing and execution succeed.
Command-history updates are omitted for clarity.
<puml src="diagrams/RollbackActivityDiagram.puml" alt="Create a rollback snapshot, execute the command and save the address book; restore the snapshot if saving fails" />
If saving throws an `IOException`, including `AccessDeniedException`, `LogicManager` restores the snapshot
and throws a `CommandException` with the save error. `ModelManager` restores students, classes, memberships,
attendance and command history, along with the previous filters, student sort order and attendance display.
The command box retains the failed input without adding it to successful command history.
Snapshots are single-use, and filter predicates must avoid capturing mutable model objects because restoration
replaces them.
The current rollback implementation handles complete save failures, where no data is written, but does not
handle recovery of partially saved files. This is [noted in the User Guide](UserGuide.md#known-issues)
and should be addressed in future iterations.

**Target user profile**:

### Non-Functional Requirements
| ID | Category | Non-Functional Requirement |
| NFR01 | Usability | TAssist should be optimised for users who are comfortable with typing, with typed commands as the primary means of interacting with the application. |
| NFR02 | Performance | TAssist should respond to normal user commands within 2 seconds under typical usage conditions. |
| NFR03 | Capacity | TAssist should support at least 500 students across 20 classes and 10 modules while maintaining normal command response times. |

| NFR04 | Data Persistence | Every successful operation that modifies application data should be automatically saved to local storage so that the latest data remains available after the application is restarted. |

| NFR05 | Data Integrity | A failed or invalid operation should not result in partially modified or inconsistent application data. Existing valid data should remain unchanged if the operation cannot be completed successfully. |

| NFR06 | Error Handling | When an invalid command or input is entered, TAssist should provide a clear error message that identifies the problem and, where appropriate, indicates the expected command format. |
| NFR07 | Single-User Operation | TAssist should operate as a single-user application and should not support multiple users accessing the same application data during normal operation. |
| NFR08 | Data Storage | TAssist data should be stored locally in a human-editable text file and should not rely on a database management system. |
| NFR09 | Platform Compatibility | TAssist should work on Windows, Linux, and macOS without relying on operating-system-specific functionality. |
| NFR10 | Runtime Compatibility | TAssist should be compatible with Java 25. |
| NFR11 | Portability | TAssist should run without requiring an installer and should be distributed as a single JAR file, or a single ZIP file if additional files are unavoidable. |
| NFR12 | Offline Availability | Core TAssist functionality should not depend on the team's own remote server and should remain usable without an Internet connection. |

| NFR13 | Display Compatibility | The GUI should work without resolution-related inconvenience at 1920×1080 or above at 100%/125% scaling, and all functionality should remain usable at 1280×720 or above at 150% scaling. |
### Glossary
| Term | Definition |
| TAssist | The application developed to help teaching assistants manage student contacts and information across the classes they teach. |
| TA | Teaching Assistant. The primary target user of TAssist. |
| Student | A person whose contact and class information is managed by a TA using TAssist. |
| Student Number | The unique institutional identifier used by TAssist to identify a student. |
| Module | An academic course taught by the TA, identified by its module code, such as `CS2103`. A module may contain one or more classes. |
| Class | A tutorial or lab group belonging to a module, identified by a class name such as `F10-2`. A class is uniquely identified by its combination of module and class name. |
| Student Profile | The information stored about a student, such as their student number, name, email address, Telegram username, and class associations. |
| Communication Handle | Contact information used to communicate with a student, such as their email address or Telegram username. |
| CLI | Command-Line Interface. The text-based interface through which the user enters commands in TAssist. |
| Command | A textual instruction entered into TAssist to perform an operation, such as `addstudent`, `find`, or `assign`. |
| Command Prefix | A prefix used to specify a parameter in a command, such as `sn/` for student number, `m/` for module, or `c/` for class. |

5. Repeat the scrolling checks after `listbyclass CLASS_INDEX`, replacing `CLASS_INDEX` with a
displayed class containing enough assigned students to scroll. Include students with no
attendance dates and students with enough dates to wrap over several lines.
Expected: attendance remains below the contact details and tags, inside the correct card.
6. Click a panel heading or background, or use Tab/Shift+Tab to focus its list, then press Up/Down.
Expected: only the focused list scrolls; records remain unselected and unchanged.
### Listing classes by student
1. Add students and classes using unused identifiers:
`add sn/A0999801X n/AlphaDemoAlice e/alpha.demo.alice@example.com`,
`add sn/A0999802Y n/AlphaDemoBob e/alpha.demo.bob@example.com`,
`addclass m/CS2103 c/DEMO-T01`, and `addclass m/CS2100 c/DEMO-L01`.
2. Run `list` and `listclass`. Check Alice's displayed student index and the two displayed class indices.
Assign her using `assign STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX` for each class.
3. Run `find AlphaDemoAlice`, then `listbystudent 1`.
Expected: both classes appear in creation order; feedback reports two classes and Alice's identity.
The student search results remain unchanged.
4. Run `listbystudent 0`, `listbystudent 1 extra`, and `listbystudent 2`.
Expected: invalid-command or invalid-index feedback; both views remain unchanged.
5. Run `unassign 1 1`.
Expected: only CS2100 DEMO-L01 remains in the Classes panel.
6. Run `find AlphaDemoBob`, then `listbystudent 1`.
Expected: zero matching classes and an empty Classes panel.
7. Run `listclass` to restore all classes, and `list` to restore all students.
Restart the app and repeat Alice's lookup to verify that memberships persist while display filters reset.
### Listing students by class and recording attendance
Use a separate JAR copy in a disposable, writable folder. Run the following setup once, then follow
these checks in order. `clear` deletes that copy's records; do not use real data.
```text
clear
add sn/A0999801X n/Zoe Test e/zoe.test@example.com
add sn/A0999802Y n/Alice Test e/alice.test@example.com
addclass m/CS2103 c/TEST-A
addclass m/CS2100 c/TEST-B
assign 1 1
assign 2 1
Expected: Zoe then Alice appear in insertion order; TEST-A has both students and TEST-B is empty.
Student and class indices refer to their respective displayed panels.
| Commands (run in order) | Expected result |
| `listbyclass 2`, then `listbyclass 1` | The empty class shows no students. Switching back shows Alice (1), then Zoe (2), alphabetically. Both classes remain displayed. |

| `listbystudent 1`, then `addattendance 1 2 d/2024-02-29`, then `listclass` | Only TEST-A is displayed after filtering classes for Alice. Class index 2 is rejected even though TEST-B exists in storage; no attendance is recorded. `listclass` restores both classes. |
| `addattendance 1 1 d/2025-02-29` | The impossible calendar date is rejected without recording attendance. |
| `addattendance 1 1 d/2024-02-29` | Alice gains one attendance date, although Zoe was first in insertion order. Her card shows the date under Feb 2024. |
| Repeat `addattendance 1 1 d/2024-02-29` | Duplicate attendance is rejected; Alice still has one date. |
| `addattendance 999 1 d/2024-02-29` | Invalid displayed-index feedback; no attendance changes. |
| `addattendance 1 1 d/DATE`, replacing `DATE` with tomorrow's local date in `YYYY-MM-DD` format | The future date is rejected. |
| `listbyclass 1 t/1` | Only Zoe appears, because Alice no longer has fewer than one attendance date. |
| `addattendance 1 1 d/2024-03-01`, then `listbyclass 1` | Zoe gains a date and leaves the threshold view. Removing the threshold shows both students again. |

| `listbyclass 1 t/2`, then `deleteattendance 1 1 d/2024-02-29`, then `listbyclass 1 t/1` | Both students initially have fewer than two dates. Removing Alice's date keeps that filter active; the subsequent zero-attendance view shows only Alice. Her membership and Zoe's date remain. |
| Repeat `deleteattendance 1 1 d/2024-02-29` | Attendance-not-recorded feedback; no further changes. |
| `listbyclass 1` | Both students reappear: Alice (1) has zero dates and Zoe (2) has one. Use these indices for the unassignment checks below. |
To check retained attendance after unassignment:
1. Run `unassign 2 1`, then `list`. Zoe leaves the class view; `list` restores Zoe (1), then Alice (2).
1. Run `addattendance 1 1 d/2024-03-02`. Expected: rejected because Zoe is no longer assigned.
1. Run `deleteattendance 1 1 d/2024-03-01`, then `assign 1 1` and `listbyclass 1`.
Expected: the retained date can be removed without reassignment; both students finish assigned with zero dates.
### Preserving student filters after changes
Continue from the setup above after completing the attendance checks:
1. Run `find Alice`, then `add sn/A0999812Y n/Bob Test e/bob.filter@example.com`.
Expected: Bob is stored but hidden by the search; Alice remains visible.
1. Run `add sn/A0999813Z n/Alice Other e/alice.other@example.com`.
Expected: the matching student appears as student 2 without clearing the search.
1. Run `edit 2 n/Carol Other`, then `delete 1`.
Expected: Carol leaves the results, then deleting Alice leaves the view empty rather than revealing other students.
1. Run `list`. Expected: Zoe, Bob and Carol appear; the nonmatching records were retained.
### Saving data
Use disposable folders and keep a backup before changing files or permissions. Close the main window
before editing files, except in the permission-failure check, which needs the same session to remain open.
1. **Save and restart:** Repeat the attendance setup in a fresh folder. Run `listbyclass 1`, then
`addattendance 1 1 d/2024-02-29`. Close and reopen the same JAR, then run `listbyclass 1`.
Expected: both memberships and Alice's date persist; TEST-B remains empty. Display filters reset on restart.
1. **JAR-relative storage:** Close the app and launch it from a different working directory using
`java -jar "ABSOLUTE_PATH_TO_TAssist.jar"` with the actual JAR path.
Expected: the same records load and the status bar points to `data/addressbook.json` beside the JAR.
Copy only the JAR to an empty writable folder and launch it; that copy should have sample data and its own path.
1. **Missing or corrupted data:** With the app closed, rename the test data file to `addressbook.backup.json`.
Restart: sample students should load. Close without entering commands, create `data/addressbook.json`
containing only `not-json`, then restart: the app should show empty data. Close without entering commands
and restore the backup as `addressbook.json`; the original records should load again.
1. **Failed-save rollback and recovery:** Keep a test instance with saved students open. Back up its data file
and deny write access to `data/addressbook.json` using actual OS permissions, recording how to restore them.
Run `delete 1`: expect a save error, with the student, memberships, attendance and displayed view restored.
The file should be unchanged because writing was denied before it started. Restore write access without
closing the app, then run `list`. Expect no save error; restart and verify that the student still exists.
This tests a denied write, not a partial write. An interrupted write can leave incomplete JSON despite
rollback; recover in the same session after resolving the storage problem, or restore a known-good backup.
1. **Write-protected launch folder:** In another folder containing only the JAR, deny file creation but retain
read/execute access. Launch from a terminal: expect no app window and an application-lock error. Restore
permissions afterward. A folder's read-only checkbox alone may not deny writes.
1. **Single-instance locking:** Keep TAssist open, then launch the same JAR from a second terminal, using
a different terminal working directory. Expect no second window and the already-running message.
Close the first instance and relaunch without deleting `tassist.lock`; expect a normal launch.
Copy only the JAR to another writable folder and launch it while the first is open; expect both instances
to run with independent data. Close both after checking.

# TAssist User Guide

TAssist is a **desktop application for NUS Teaching Assistants who need to manage the students they tutor, optimized for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI)** while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI). It gives TAs quick access to student contacts and information, helping them manage student learning outcomes from a central application.
<!-- * Table of Contents -->
<page-nav-print />
## Quick start
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Download the latest `.jar` file from [here](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-2/tp/releases).
1. Copy the file to a folder you can write to. This is the _home folder_ for TAssist and its saved files.
TAssist needs write access to this folder to launch and save data; see [Known issues](#known-issues).
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar TAssist.jar`.
Double-clicking the JAR also works on systems configured to open `.jar` files with a compatible Java installation.
If double-clicking does not launch TAssist, use the terminal command above so you can see any error messages.
Run `java -version` to check that the terminal uses Java `25` or later.
A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. The app shows students and classes in separate sections.
![Ui](images/Ui.png)
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
## Features
### Navigating the Students and Classes panels
Click a panel's heading, a card, or the surrounding panel space to focus its list. A blue
outline marks the focused list. Press **Up/Down** to scroll, **Page Up/Page Down** to move
by a page, or **Home/End** to reach the beginning or end.
From the command box, **Tab** moves through the result display, Students list, Classes list,
and back to the command box. **Shift+Tab** moves in reverse. Scrolling does not select or
change student or class records. Up/Down in the command box continues to browse command history.
<box type="info" seamless>
**Notes about the command format:**
* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add sn/STUDENT_NUMBER n/NAME`, replace `STUDENT_NUMBER` with a value such as `A0123456X` and `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* `INDEX` refers to a student or class in the relevant displayed list. Commands taking both indices use
`STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX`, in that order. `KEYWORD` in `find` is a full word in a student's name.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `n/NAME [t/TAG]` can be used as `n/John Doe t/friend` or as `n/John Doe`.
* Items followed by `...` can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]... ` may be omitted, or written as `t/friend` or `t/friend t/family`.
* Prefixed parameters can be in any order.
For example, if the command specifies `sn/STUDENT_NUMBER n/NAME e/EMAIL`, `e/EMAIL sn/STUDENT_NUMBER n/NAME` is also acceptable.
* Index-based parameters (e.g. `STUDENT_INDEX`, `CLASS_INDEX`) cannot be reordered and must stay in the position the command specifies.

For example, if the command specifies `assign STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX`, `assign CLASS_INDEX STUDENT_INDEX` will be interpreted incorrectly, with the first number treated as the student and the second as the class.
* Prefixes identify the kind of information you are providing.
For example, `n/` is used for student names, `m/` for module codes, and `c/` for class names.
* Repeated prefixes are accepted only when the command explicitly allows multiple values.
For example, `add` and `edit` accept multiple `t/TAG` values, but `addclass` accepts exactly one `m/MODULE_CODE` and one `c/CLASS_NAME`.
* Extraneous parameters for commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `list`, `exit`, and `clear`, are ignored.
For example, `help 123` is interpreted as `help`.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
</box>
### Viewing help: `help`
Shows a message explaining how to access the help page.
![help message](images/helpMessage.png)
Format: `help`
You can also open Help from the `Help` menu or by pressing `F1`. If the Help window is already open,
these actions bring it to the front and restore it if it is minimized.
### Adding a student: `add`
Adds a student to TAssist.
Format: `add sn/STUDENT_NUMBER n/NAME e/EMAIL [tg/TELEGRAM] [t/TAG]... `
<box type="tip" seamless>
**Tip:** A student can have any number of tags, including zero. Tags are supported by this build although they are not part of the current MVP feature list.
</box>
* `STUDENT_NUMBER` must contain 5 to 20 letters or digits, with no spaces or special characters. It is stored and displayed in uppercase, and must be unique.
* `NAME` must contain at least one ASCII letter (`A`–`Z`, `a`–`z`) or digit (`0`–`9`). Leading and trailing spaces are removed.
It accepts spaces, hyphens (`-`), straight apostrophes (`'`), periods (`.`), commas (`,`), and parentheses (`(` and `)`).
For example, `Anne-Marie Tan`, `Sean O'Connor`, `J. K. Tan`, `John Tan, Jr.`, and `Tan Wei Ming (Alex)` are valid names.
* To include a forward slash in a name, type **one backslash** (`\`) in its place: `n/Ravi S\O Kumar` is stored and displayed as `Ravi S/O Kumar`.
Use this form in both `add` and `edit`; literal forward slashes (`/`) in name input are rejected.
Backslashes represent slashes and cannot be stored as literal backslashes in a name.
* Curly apostrophes (`’`), middle dots (`·`), accented letters (such as `é`), other scripts, and unlisted punctuation are rejected.
Use a straight apostrophe (`'`) rather than a curly one. Blank names and names consisting only of punctuation are also rejected.

* `EMAIL` must be in the format `local-part@domain`, with no spaces, and be at most **200 characters** long (including `@` and the domain). Email comparisons are case-insensitive for duplicate checks.
* `TELEGRAM`, if provided, may start with `@`. After removing `@`, it must contain 5 to 32 letters, digits, or underscores. It must be unique, ignoring case.
* Parameters can be supplied in any order.
* Adding a student keeps the current student filter and display order. The new student appears only if they match the filter.

New students are not assigned to any class, so they will not appear in an active `listbyclass` view until assigned to that class (and must also meet any attendance threshold). Use `list` to show all students.
Examples:
* `add sn/A0123456X n/Alice Tan e/alice@u.nus.edu tg/alice_tan`
* `add sn/A0234567Y n/Benjamin Lim e/benjamin@u.nus.edu`
* `add e/chloe@u.nus.edu sn/A0345678Z tg/@chloe_ng n/Chloe Ng`
* `add sn/A0800001X n/Anne-Marie O'Connor e/anne@example.com`
* `add sn/A0800002X n/Ravi S\O Kumar e/ravi@example.com` stores and displays the name as `Ravi S/O Kumar`.
Expected output:
* `New student added: Alice Tan; Student Number: A0123456X; Email: alice@u.nus.edu; Telegram: @alice_tan`
Common errors:
* Duplicate student number: `A student with this student number already exists.`
* Duplicate email: `A student with this email already exists.`
* Invalid email format or an email longer than 200 characters: TAssist displays the email requirements and does not add the student.
* Duplicate Telegram username: `A student with this Telegram username already exists.`
* Invalid student number: `Invalid student number. Student numbers must contain 5–20 letters or digits with no spaces.`
* Invalid name:
```text
Names must contain at least one letter (A-Z, a-z) or digit (0-9). Spaces are allowed.
Allowed punctuation: hyphen (-), straight apostrophe ('), period (.), comma (,), parentheses ( ), and backslash (\).
Enter \ instead of /; it is stored and displayed as /. Non-ASCII characters and other punctuation are not allowed.
* Invalid Telegram username: `Invalid Telegram username. Usernames must contain 5–32 letters, digits, or underscores.`
### Editing a student: `edit`
Edits an existing student in TAssist.
Format: `edit INDEX [sn/STUDENT_NUMBER] [n/NAME] [e/EMAIL] [tg/TELEGRAM] [t/TAG]... `
* Edits the student at the specified `INDEX`. The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed student list. The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
* At least one of the optional fields must be provided.
* Existing values will be updated to the input values.
* When editing tags, all of the student's existing tags are removed; adding tags is not cumulative.
* To remove all of a student's tags, enter `t/` without a tag after it.
* To remove a student's Telegram username, enter `tg/` without a username after it. Omitting `tg/` keeps the existing username.
* Student number, email, and Telegram username must remain unique after editing.
* Emails follow the same format and 200-character limit as [`add`](#adding-a-student-add). Invalid emails are rejected without changing the student.
* Names follow the same character rules as [`add`](#adding-a-student-add). Use `\` for a displayed `/`, for example `edit 1 n/Ravi S\O Kumar`.

* Editing keeps the current student filter, sorting, and attendance display. A student who no longer matches a `find` search disappears from its results; changing a name in a `listbyclass` view may change their alphabetical position.
* Editing a student number preserves their class memberships and attendance history. Any active attendance threshold still applies.
* Check the displayed indexes again before your next command, as an edit may change which students are shown and their indexes. Use `list` to show all students.
Examples:
*  `edit 1 tg/john_doe e/johndoe@example.com` edits the Telegram username and email address of the 1st student.
*  `edit 1 tg/` removes the Telegram username of the 1st student.
*  `edit 2 sn/A0234567Y n/Benjamin Lim t/` edits the student number and name of the 2nd student, and clears all existing tags.
### Deleting a student: `delete`
Deletes the specified student from TAssist.
Format: `delete INDEX`
* Deletes the student at the specified `INDEX`.
* The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed student list.
* The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
* Deleting keeps the current student filter, sorting, and attendance display. If no remaining students match, the student list stays empty instead of showing unrelated students.
* Check the displayed indexes again before deleting another student, as the remaining students are renumbered. Use `list` to show all students.
Examples:
* `list` followed by `delete 2` deletes the 2nd student in TAssist.
* `find Betsy` followed by `delete 1` deletes the 1st student in the results of the `find` command.
Expected output:
* `Deleted student: Alice Tan; Student Number: A0123456X; Email: alice@u.nus.edu; Telegram: @alice_tan`
<box type="warning" seamless>
The current build deletes students by displayed list index, not by student number. The MVP command `deletestudent sn/STUDENT_NUMBER` is not available in this build.
</box>
### Listing all students: `list`
Shows a list of all students in TAssist.
Format: `list`
Expected output: `Listed all students.`
The student list displays each student's name, student number, email, optional Telegram username, and tags.
This command leaves the current class filter unchanged. Use `listclass` to restore all classes as well.
### Locating students by name: `find`
Finds students whose names contain any of the given keywords.
Format: `find KEYWORD [MORE_KEYWORDS]...`
* At least one keyword must be provided.
* The search considers all stored students, regardless of the students currently displayed, and replaces the current student filter.
* The search is case-insensitive; for example, `hans` matches `Hans`.
* The search considers only names.
* Only full words match; for example, `Han` does not match `Hans`.
* Students matching at least one keyword are returned (an `OR` search); for example, `Hans Bo` returns both `Hans Gruber` and `Bo Yang`.
* Keyword order does not matter; for example, `Hans Bo` produces the same results as `Bo Hans`.
* Punctuation remains part of a word. Use `Anne-Marie` rather than `Anne` to match `Anne-Marie`, or `O'Connor` to match `O'Connor`.
For `John Tan, Jr. (Alex)`, search with `Tan,` or `(Alex)`; `Tan` and `Alex` do not match those words.
* For a displayed slash, either input form works: `find S\O` and `find S/O` both match the word `S/O`.
* Results are displayed in their original insertion order.
* Running `find` clears any active `listbyclass` attendance threshold and attendance display.
* The displayed class list and its current filter remain unchanged. Use `listclass` to show all classes.
The result message reports the number of matching students, including when no students match:
`N student(s) listed!`
Examples:
* `find John` returns students whose names contain the full word `John`, such as `john` and `John Doe`.
* `find alex david` returns `Alex Yeoh` and `David Li`.
![Result for `find alex david`](images/findAlexDavidResult.png)
### Listing all classes: `listclass`
Shows all academic classes in creation order and clears the class filter set by `listbystudent`.
The displayed student list is unchanged.
Format: `listclass`
Expected output: `Listed all classes.` Extra arguments are rejected.
The student and class filters can be reset independently:
| Command | Students panel | Classes panel |
| `list` | Shows all students | Keeps the current class filter |
| `listclass` | Keeps the current student filter | Shows all classes, including empty classes |
Run `list` followed by `listclass` to restore both complete lists.
### Assigning a student to a class: `assign`
Assigns an existing student to an existing academic class.
Format: `assign STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX`
* Put the student index first and the class index second. Both must be positive integers from their respective displayed lists.
* `STUDENT_INDEX` uses the current Students panel, including `find` and `listbyclass` results.
* `CLASS_INDEX` uses the current Classes panel, including `listbystudent` results.
* The student and class must already exist and be visible. Use `list` and `listclass` to restore the complete lists if needed.
* Check the displayed indices after filtering, editing records, changing memberships, or recalling a previous command.
* Assignment preserves active filters. Membership-based views and class student counts update automatically.
* After a successful assignment, both panels scroll to the affected student and class, provided they remain in the displayed results. Keyboard focus stays in the command box.
* A student may belong to multiple classes. Repeating an assignment reports that the student is already assigned and leaves the membership unchanged.
Example:
* `assign 1 2` assigns the first displayed student to the second displayed class.
Expected output (if the selected student is `A1111111H` and the class is `CS2103 F-10`):
* `Student (A1111111H) has been assigned to CS2103-F-10.`
Common errors:
* Missing, extra, zero, negative, non-integer, or prefixed arguments: `Invalid command format!` followed by the command usage.
* Student index outside the displayed list: `The student index provided is invalid.`
* Class index outside the displayed list: `The class index provided is invalid.`
* Student already assigned: `Student (A1234567H) is already assigned to class CS2101-L1.`
Rejected commands leave memberships and student counts unchanged.
![Screenshot highlighting student assignment to class](images/assign-result.png)
### Unassigning a student from an academic class: `unassign`
Removes a student's membership from one academic class. The student remains in the address book and in other classes.
Format: `unassign STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX`
* Both indices are required positive integers, in student-then-class order, counting from `1` in their respective displayed panels.
* The student and class must be visible, and the student must already be assigned to that class.
* After `find`, `listbyclass`, or `listbystudent`, use the indices in the current results. Run `list` to restore all students or `listclass` to restore all classes if the target is hidden.
* Only membership in the selected class is removed. Student and class records, other memberships, and recorded attendance history are retained.
* Active filters and ordering are preserved. Membership-dependent views refresh, so a student or class may disappear and remaining indices may shift.

* After a successful unassignment, both panels scroll to the affected student and class if they remain displayed. A record removed by an active filter stays hidden; the panel does not scroll to a different record in its place. Keyboard focus stays in the command box.
* Check both panels before repeating a command. Reusing the same indices after a view changes can target a different student or class.
Example: suppose student `A1111111H` is displayed at student index `2` and `CS2103-F10` is displayed at class index `1`:
```text
unassign 2 1
Expected feedback:
```text
Student (A1111111H) has been unassigned from CS2103-F10.
**Example walkthrough**
Use a fresh data folder with no existing records so the indices below match. Enter each command separately.
```text
clear
add sn/A0999801X n/AlphaDemoAlice e/alpha.demo.alice@example.com
addclass m/CS2103 c/DEMO-T01
assign 1 1
listbyclass 1
unassign 1 1
Expected feedback: `Student (A0999801X) has been unassigned from CS2103-DEMO-T01.`
The class remains in the Classes panel with `Students: 0`. The Students panel becomes empty because
the active view only shows members of that class. Run `list` to see Alice again; her student record has not been deleted.
Common errors:
* Missing, extra, or invalid indices (including zero, negative numbers, decimals, and the old prefixes): `Invalid command format!` followed by the command usage.
* Student index outside the displayed list: `The student index provided is invalid.`
* Class index outside the displayed list: `The class index provided is invalid.`

* Student not assigned to the selected class: `Student (A1234567H) is not assigned to class CS2101-L1.` Repeating an unassignment produces this error only if the indices still identify the same student and class.
Rejected commands leave memberships and student counts unchanged.
![Screenshot highlighting student unassignment from class](images/unassign-result.png)
### Listing students by class: `listbyclass`
Shows only students assigned to the class at the specified displayed index, alphabetically by name using the existing
student cards.
Each card also shows the dates on which that student attended the class.
Optionally, specify `t/THRESHOLD` to filter for class members with fewer than `THRESHOLD` recorded attendance dates in that class.
Format: `listbyclass INDEX [t/THRESHOLD]`
* `INDEX` must be a positive integer referring to a class in the displayed class list.
* `THRESHOLD` (optional) must be a positive integer.
* When `t/THRESHOLD` is provided, only students assigned to the selected class with **fewer than `THRESHOLD` recorded attendance dates** for that class are displayed.

* Students with no recorded attendance for that class count as having `0` attendance dates (for example, `t/1` displays only students with `0` recorded dates, and `t/5` displays students with `0` to `4` recorded dates while excluding students with `5` or more dates).
* Attendance recorded for other classes does not affect the count for the selected class.
* Omitting `t/THRESHOLD` lists all students assigned to the class and clears any active attendance threshold restriction.
* The class list index is independent of the student list index.
* An invalid or out-of-range index or threshold is rejected without changing the student list.
* Names are sorted ignoring case, with original spelling used to break ties.
* Adding or deleting attendance dates, or assigning/unassigning students, immediately updates the displayed list against the active class and threshold filter.
* An existing class with no matching students shows an empty student list and a count of zero.
* Deleting the class currently being displayed empties the student list without deleting student records.
If you recreate the class, subsequent assignments update this view using the new class membership.
If you rename another class to the deleted class's module code and class name, the student list immediately
shows that class's members in alphabetical order, subject to any active attendance threshold.
* Renaming the class currently being displayed with `editclass` preserves both the class view and any active `t/THRESHOLD` attendance filter.
* This command changes only the displayed student list, not student records, class memberships, or the class list.
* Use `list` to show all students again. `list` and `find` display results in their original insertion order.
Examples:

* Check the class list displayed in the UI, then run `listbyclass 1` to list all students in the 1st displayed class, or `listbyclass 1 t/5` to list only students in the 1st displayed class with fewer than 5 recorded attendance dates.
The result message includes the student count and class (and the threshold when specified), for example:
* `Listed 2 students taking CS2103 (F10-2).`
* `Listed 1 student taking CS2103 (F10-2) with fewer than 5 recorded attendance dates.`
Classes created with `addclass` start empty. Use `assign STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX`
to assign an existing student before listing the class. Memberships are saved across restarts.

### Recording attendance: `addattendance`
Records one attended date for a student in a particular module and class.
Format: `addattendance STUDENT_INDEX CLASS_INDEX d/YYYY-MM-DD`

* `STUDENT_INDEX` selects a student in the current displayed student list, including `find` and `listbyclass` results.
`CLASS_INDEX` selects a class in the current displayed class list, including `listbystudent` results.
* Put the student index first and the class index second, followed by exactly one `d/` date.
Both indices must be positive integers within their respective displayed lists.
Missing, extra, zero, negative, non-integer and out-of-range indices are rejected.
* Check both displayed indices again after changing views, editing data or changing class membership,
including when recalling an old command. The same indices may now refer to a different student or class.
* Student-number input (`sn/`), module/class prefixes (`m/`, `c/`) and other unknown prefixes are rejected.
Extra whitespace between the indices and around the date is accepted.
* Use a valid calendar date with a year from `0001` to `9999`, a two-digit month and a two-digit day.
Today and past dates are accepted; future dates are rejected using your computer's local date.
* Recording the same date twice for the same student and class is rejected without changing the existing record.
Other students and classes have separate attendance histories.
* Recording attendance preserves the active student and class filters. The student list refreshes to reflect the new attendance.
With `listbyclass CLASS_INDEX t/THRESHOLD`, a student disappears if their attendance count reaches the threshold.
For example, a student with no recorded dates disappears from a `t/1` view after their first date is recorded.
Check the displayed indices again before your next command, as remaining students may be renumbered.
* Successful records are saved automatically and retained after restarting TAssist.
Unassigning a student keeps their history, but new dates cannot be recorded until they are assigned again.
Deleting the student or class removes the associated attendance history.
